headlines.title: Former Warriors coach, Naismith Basketball Hall of Famer Don Nelson dead at 86
headlines.description: Some, giggling at some of his imaginative lineups, called him the mad scientist of the NBA. Others considered him cunning, even ruthless, a shrewd behind-the-scenes manipulator with a gift for obscuring his ulterior motives with a smile or a joke. Don Nelson was all that and more. The former Golden State Warriors coach who in 2012 entered the Naismith Memorial Hall of Fame, died Sunday at age 86. It is conceivable that no coach in NBA history did more moving and shaking and feuding, on the court and off, than Nelson. No coach did more winning, either, until one of Nelson’s disciples, San Antonio’s Gregg Popovich, supplanted him atop the NBA’s career wins list in March 2022. “Don Nelson was a true innovator whose influence on the game of basketball is still felt today,” Warriors coach Steve Kerr wrote in a statement. “He consistently challenged conventional thinking, experimented with different lineups and styles of play and saw possibilities in the game that others often did not. So much of what is now commonplace in the modern NBA can be traced back to the way Nellie approached the game. His impact on the Warriors is just as significant. He helped shape some of the most memorable teams and moments in franchise history and built a lasting connection with generations of Warriors fans. His legacy will always remain an important part of this organization. My thoughts are with the entire Nelson family.” “One of the big reasons I was drafted by the Warriors was because of Don Nelson,” Warriors superstar Steph Curry wrote. “The story is he never liked rookies, but from Day 1 he challenged me and gave me an opportunity to be my best self on the court. He taught me a lot during our one season together and I’ll never forget the night he became the winningest coach in NBA history in Minnesota. We were so happy for him. He had an immeasurable impact on the sport and will go down as one of the greatest minds in the history of the game. He’s a true icon and will be missed by the countless number of people he touched, including myself, during a legendary career. Sending my love to Joy, his family and all those who were fortunate enough to know him.” Nelson was the first coach to make copious use of a “point forward,” running plays through Marques Johnson and Paul Pressey in Milwaukee, though Rod Higgins and Chris Mullin and Stephen Jackson in Golden State. Nelson displayed considerable ingenuity with schemes that generated offense but never devoted much attention to defense. Which is how Nelson executed one of the great magic tricks in sports. He retired in 2010 with more wins than any coach the league had ever known yet never won a championship or reached The Finals. Nelson spent 31 seasons coaching four different NBA teams, serving two terms with the Warriors – 1988-94, 2007-10 – both of which mixed excitement before devolving into controversy or animosity. As Golden State coach/general manager in the late 1980s and early ‘90s, Nelson was the architect of the fabled Run-TMC teams featuring Hall of Famers Tim Hardaway, Mitch Richmond and Chris Mullin. After so many sub-mediocre seasons, the enthusiasm for those teams made Nelson a Bay Area celebrity so popular that he would receive standing ovations at the Oakland Coliseum Arena when walking onto the court before tipoff. Yet it was Nelson who, after coaching Run-TMC for two seasons, the second of which included a first-round playoff sweep of the Utah Jazz, dismantled the trio by trading Richmond. The move blew up the team’s strong chemistry. It took 16 years, with eight coaches cycling through the franchise, for the Warriors to win another postseason series; Nelson later acknowledged the trade was his biggest regret. Yes, even bigger than his mismanagement of Chris Webber. The first overall pick in the 1993 draft lasted one season, in which he was named Rookie of the Year. Nelson, headstrong, made few sincere attempts to connect with the big man of his dreams and their differences quickly became irreconcilable. The Warriors were swept by Phoenix in the first round of the 1994 playoffs. Webber was traded within six months, with Nelson resigning three months later. Eighteen months after Golden State was positioned to become a perennial playoff team, the franchise plummeted to its nadir, with Webber getting some of the blame but the brunt of it directed at Nelson. After one uneasy season coaching the New York Knicks, Nelson took a year off before being hired by the Dallas Mavericks. After three sub-.500 seasons, Nelson guided a roster featuring Steve Nash and young Dirk Nowitzki to four consecutive playoff berths, including his first conference finals. That run also ended bitterly, with Nelson and high-profile team owner Mark Cuban accusing each other of lies and deceit. Nelson filed a lawsuit than ended with him receiving a $6.3 million settlement through arbitration. By which time Nelson had returned to the Warriors – and taken them to the playoffs. Mullin, then the general manager, persuaded his former coach, then 66, to return to the sideline. Mullin then made a midseason trade to acquire Stephen Jackson and Al Harrington, who along with incumbent point guard Baron Davis, presenting Nelson with a satisfying roster that finished 42-40 and became the “We Believe” Warriors. Earning the No. 8 seed, they achieved one of the biggest upsets in playoff history, taking down the top-seeded Mavericks. It was a particularly tasty triumph for the coach. The euphoria lasted one season. Though the Warriors made significant improvement in the regular season, finishing 48-34, their efforts went for naught in an exceedingly rare season in which eight teams in the West won at least 50 games. A few months later, Nelson and Davis were at odds, with Mullin in the uncomfortable role of referee – while also trying to re-sign in the point guard. Golden State president Robert Rowell nixed the Davis deal, which led to friction among all involved parties. Nelson lasted two more seasons, both wretched. Through it all, Nelson retired as the most imaginative coach the Warriors had ever known. Moreover, he left them with a gift that serves as glorious restitution for his sins: Nelson selected a point guard named Stephen Curry in the first round of the 2009 draft. headlines.title: Timber Fire burns over 300 acres in Monterey County, prompts evacuation warning
headlines.description: A fire burning south of Loma Vista in Monterey County has prompted an evacuation warning Sunday, according to the Monterey County Sheriff’s Office. The sheriff’s office said it issued an evacuation warning related to the fire, named Timber Fire, for areas of Big Sur near Partington Ridge Road and North Coast Ridge Road, for the MRY-F026 and MRY-F027 zones. According to Cal Fire, the Timber Fire has already burned 400 acres and was 20% contained. The sheriff’s office added the evacuation warning excluded the Ventana Inn. The cause of the fire is unknown.

headlines.title: Phone ban at Oakland Unified to go into effect
headlines.description: Quite a few Bay Area school districts start their new year on Monday, including Oakland Unified, where schools will have new cell phone restrictions. It’s part of a statewide mandate requiring districts to have policies limiting or banning the use of cell phones on campus. Some school districts across the state, including San Jose Unified, began implementing their own policies in 2025. Oakland Unified is one of the last major school districts to roll this out. OUSD alerted families that the new cell phone rules will begin on Monday when classes start. The district said that generally, elementary school kids will keep phones in locked classroom boxes. Middle and high school students will store cell phones in special Yondr pouches during the school day, which they can carry with them, but can’t unlock until the end of the school day. The district says phones will also be allowed for documented medical needs and individual education plans. Staff can unlock phones that have been locked away if there’s an emergency as well. Some parents and students NBC Bay Area spoke with on Sunday were generally in favor of the policy. “Kids should not have phones at school, especially when they’re trying to learn,” said Charlie An, a parent of an OUSD elementary school student. “Phones, I think, just take their attention away from learning and being able to absorb critical information that they need form school,” he continued.

headlines.title: 2 pedestrians hurt after being struck by a pickup truck in San Francisco
headlines.description: Two people were taken to the hospital after being struck by a pickup truck in San Francisco on Sunday, according to the fire department. Authorities said a pickup truck hit two pedestrians and crashed into a light pole shortly before 12:30 p.m. on O’Farrell and Cyril Magnin streets. The pedestrians were taken to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, according to the fire department. They added two people in the truck were treated and released at the scene. The fire department said the police department is investigating the cause of the crash.

headlines.title: Festivals in San Francisco draw thousands of people to the city over the weekend
headlines.description: The Outside Lands Music Festival drew tens of thousands of people to Golden Gate Park over three days, but there were other events, including music at the Stern Grove Festival. In San Francisco, people lined up to see a performance at Stern Grove with an artist they’ve been waiting to see. For a fan, the choice of getting to the city from the East Bay did not involve driving. “I caught BART and Muni, but I actually had a smooth stop, I got off at St. Francisco circle and came off,” Tanna said. Sunday was the last day of this year’s Outside Lands Music Festival at Golden Gate Park. The festival was expected to draw a quarter of a million people over the three-day weekend, with a list of favorites. For Outside Lands, people could take special metro shuttles or the Judah Muni Line. Rideshare has drop-off spots and autonomous vehicles are restricted to rides a few blocks away from the park. SFMTA says it’s been going well getting people in and out efficiently. Across town, the annual Pistahan Parade and Festival returned to the city over the weekend. “This is the only Filipino festival here in San Francisco, so the community knows that this is the time for us to come together celebrate our roots uplift our community and enjoy some Filipino food and some entertainment,” Filipino American Arts Exposition President Al Perez said.

headlines.title: Silver Alert issued for missing San Francisco man with dementia
headlines.description: A Silver Alert has been issued for a 65-year-old San Francisco man with dementia who has been missing since Saturday afternoon. Jason Chen was last seen at approximately 2:17 p.m. on Saturday, Aug. 8, near Third Street and McKinnon Avenue, according to authorities and his family. He is considered an at-risk adult and is believed to be traveling on foot. Family members expressed extreme concern for his safety and are pleading for the public’s help in locating him. Chen is described as 5 feet, 6 inches tall and 167 pounds, with black hair and brown eyes. He was last seen wearing a gray-and-blue sweater over a black hoodie and blue jeans. Anyone who spots Chen is urged to immediately call 911. Individuals can also reach out to his family directly with any information. His relative, Alton Chen, can be contacted at 650-270-0951 or via email atalton.sf.ca@gmail.com.

headlines.title: Report: Group in deadly avalanche near Lake Tahoe tried to avoid risky path
headlines.description: A report detailing what went wrong during a deadly avalanche in the sierra this past winter was released on Sunday. The Feb. 17 avalanche near “Perry Peak” in the Truckee area killed nine people, and sparked questions about why the group left their ski huts in a snowstorm, with active avalanche warnings. The 68-page preliminary report found that the guides decided to leave during a break in the storm, on the last day of what was supposed to be three days of back-country deep-powder skiing. Before going into the path of the avalanche, GPS data shows the group made multiple attempts to avoid the riskiest part of the avalanche zone by crossing a creek that is usually covered in snow, but they were blocked by open water and steep creek banks and were forced to go back to the other exit trail. The report was written by a veteran mountaineer and risk consultant who formerly operated the American Avalanche Institute in Colorado. headlines.title: Heat advisory and coastal flood advisory issued for the Bay Area through Sunday
headlines.description: The National Weather Service issued a heat advisory Saturday for the interior Bay Area and Central Coast through Sunday night. The NWS also issued a coastal flood advisory for Bayshore locations through Thursday. High temperatures are forecast to be in the 90s and up to 105 degrees Fahrenheit in some interior parts of the region, according to the advisory. Lows are forecast to be in the 60s to 80s. The advisory was active in parts of all Bay Area and Central Coast counties from Monterey to Sonoma, except Marin County. Links to cooling centers or plans to operate them in each county are available through the California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services website. The Weather Service recommended avoiding strenuous outdoor activities, staying hydrated, and shifting outdoor labor to evening or morning hours when it will be cooler than midday. Pet owners should take precautions not to leave animals in vehicles. A coastal flood advisory was also issued for the Bayshore locations along the San Francisco Bay, San Pablo Bay and Monterey Bay through Thursday at 2 a.m., warning of high tides of up to 1.6 ft. and flooding of lots, parks and roads.
headlines.source: Bay City News and NBC Bay Area staff

headlines.title: Half-acre fire shuts down Monterey County's Jacks Peak Park
headlines.description: Jacks Peak Park in Monterey County was closed to hikers, picnickers and horseback riders on Sunday after a fire broke out on Saturday. The fire was kept to about half an acre by Cal Fire crews and firefighters from the Monterey County Regional Fire Protection District, Carmel Highlands Fire Protection District, and city of Monterey. It broke out just before 5 p.m. off Jacks Peak Road in the forested park that is a popular recreation destination. The park off state Highway 68 has about 8.5 miles of hiking trails and borders the city of Monterey to the southeast. Forward progress on the fire was stopped at about 6 p.m., according to Cal Fire. Crews continued to do mop up duty throughout the day, which involves fortifying containment lines, monitoring for hotspots, and churning up soil and vegetation to ensure the fire isn’t burning underneath cover. The park’s closure could extend into Monday, according to a statement from Monterey County.

headlines.title: 49ers icon Roger Craig shares vascular dementia diagnosis in Hall of Fame speech
headlines.description: Legendary running back Roger Craig made a startling disclosure Saturday during his pre-recorded acceptance speech into the Pro Football Hall of Fame. Toward the end of his 10-minute address, Craig revealed he has been diagnosed with vascular dementia. Vascular dementia, the second-most common dementia diagnosis behind Alzheimer’s, is caused by conditions that limit blood flow to the brain and can lead to problems with memory, thinking, and behavior. Craig, 66, played 11 seasons in the NFL from 1983 to ’93. He played for the 49ers during his first eight seasons as a professional. “Today, there is another chapter I want to share,” Craig said in his remarks that were played at Tom Benson Hall of Fame Stadium in Canton, Ohio, and broadcast to a national-television audience. “I’ve been diagnosed with vascular dementia that my doctors believe may be related, at least in part, to the concussions I experienced during my career.” Craig had not spoken publicly since his election was announced as one of the five-person Class of 2026 on Feb. 5 during the NFL Honors show at the Palace of Fine Arts in San Francisco. Craig said his condition worsened gradually over time and was initially dismissed as normal aging. He spoke candidly about the dichotomy between all football gave him and the potential risks of playing the game. “Two things could be true,” Craig said. “Football gave me opportunities beyond anything I can imagine. It helped shape the man I became. At the same time, we know more today about brain health than when I played. And I hope sharing my story encourages people to pay attention to their health and seek help when something doesn’t feel right.” Craig exhibited all of the positive attributes that made him one of the 49ers’ most popular players at a time when both sides of the ball were stacked with other star players. “I want people to know this diagnosis doesn’t define me,” he said. “I am still Roger Craig. I am still a father, a husband, a teammate, a friend, and someone who loves this game, and the people who brought it to my life. “If sharing my story helps even one family or one former player, then it’s worth it. Football gave me everything: Opportunity, discipline, lifelong friends, and the platform to grow as a man.” Download and follow the 49ers Talk Podcast

headlines.title: Forward progress stopped on vegetation fire in South San Jose
headlines.description: Firefighters were battling a vegetation fire in South San Jose on Saturday. At 12:05 p.m., Cal Fire SCU said on X the blaze was reported in the 9500 block of Malech Road in South San Jose, near the Santa Clara County Sheriff’s Office shooting range. Initially, the fire had burned 3 acres, but it later grew to 25 acres, authorities said. At 1:19 p.m., Cal Fire reported the forward progress of the fire was stopped, and the flames ended up burning 32 acres. headlines.title: 1 cat killed in SF structure fire on Cordova Street
headlines.description: The San Francisco Fire Department responded to 47 Cordova St. after reports of fire on the second floor of a two-story, single-family residential home, Sunday morning. According to SFFD’s social media post, around 2:57 a.m., multiple occupants have self-evacuated, with two people receiving non-life-threatening injuries. Additionally, multiple pets have been rescued from the fire, firefighters said. Unfortunately, one cat had died. The fire was under control, but the SFFD is assessing how many occupants will be displaced. The American Red Cross and city services will provide aid. Firefighters said the cause of the fire is under investigation.
